query: Taking nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as the starting material, what single intervention could prevent its radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication? Formulate one testable hypothesis for energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service, including comparison with the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa; identify the intervention and mechanism, predict quantitative or directional changes in precipitation, irradiation defects, and hardening, define the applicable irradiation and thermal boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing about 7–8 at% Hf into the starting nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy will suppress the radiation‐induced formation of Cr–V nanoprecipitates while preserving its negligible irradiation hardening and simultaneously improving its ability to be fabricated in bulk form.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11, a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy that under irradiation (~8 dpa) develops fine (~3–5 nm), uniformly distributed Cr–V–rich precipitates yet shows only minor increases in hardness.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by doping with approximately 7–8 atomic percent Hf to form a quinary W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf alloy.
generation.conditions: Energetic-particle irradiation experiments simulating fusion environments at doses near 8 dpa and temperatures around 1073 K.
generation.structural_mediator: The added Hf alters the short-range chemical order and shifts the order-disorder transition temperature (ODTT), promoting a more homogenized elemental distribution under irradiation.
generation.mechanism: Hf induces greater lattice distortion and modifies the mixing enthalpies; these changes reduce the thermodynamic driving force for Cr–V phase separation by suppressing elemental partitioning, thereby inhibiting nanoprecipitate nucleation without impairing the defect sink characteristics that maintain negligible irradiation hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical irradiation conditions, the Hf-doped alloy will exhibit a marked reduction or near elimination of Cr–V precipitates, maintain low irradiation hardening comparable to the unmodified alloy, and display enhanced sinterability and bulk processing characteristics.
generation.baseline: The original nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 alloy shows the formation of ≈3–5 nm Cr–V precipitates (density ~0.03 nm⁻²) and only slight irradiation-induced hardening at around 8 dpa.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions of energetic-particle irradiation up to ~8 dpa at temperatures near 1073 K; outside these conditions (e.g., much lower or higher temperatures, or significantly different doses), the balance of phase stability and defect kinetics might differ.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Hf content and its influence on mechanical properties in a bulk-fabricated product require further quantification, and the interplay between grain-boundary-mediated defect dynamics and modified chemical ordering remains to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 (control) and a second set with ~7–8 at% Hf added to form the quinary alloy. Subject both sets to energetic-particle irradiation up to ~8 dpa at approximately 1073 K. After irradiation, perform systematic microstructural and mechanical evaluations.
measurements: Atom probe tomography (APT) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to determine precipitate size, density, and elemental distribution.
Nanoindentation or other hardness measurements to assess irradiation-induced hardening.
Evaluation of bulk fabrication properties (e.g., density, grain homogeneity) via standard metallurgical characterization.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the Hf-doped alloy exhibits similar or increased Cr–V precipitation relative to the control, shows significantly altered (e.g., increased) irradiation hardening, or if its bulk fabrication characteristics do not improve compared to the unmodified alloy.

The striations contained two main layers, a W-Ta layer, and a Cr-V-Hf layer. The present work shows the development of a new class of a refractory HEA based on four elements: 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V in atomic percentages measured by both EDS and APT. Samples were grown using a magnetron sputtering deposition system from pure metal targets and characterized before and after irradiation. Microstructures present a single-phase BCC crystalline structure. The films show a bimodal grain size distribution with ~70% of the grains with sizes in the nanocrystalline regime (≤100 nm) and some regions of ultrafine grain sizes (100 to 500 nm). Concurrent TEM and APT analyses demonstrate the existence of a second phase rich in Cr and V, first forming lamella-like regions to transform to quasi-spherical precipitates after irradiation. Irradiations were carried out both in situ and ex situ at room temperature and 1073 K up to 8 dpa. A thorough analysis of the microstructure shows no sign of radiation-induced dislocation loops, confirming that the observed black spots are indeed second-phase particles.
